questions.question: Two libraries each ship a class named `Utils`, and the project must use both without a name clash — in Java, which mechanism namespaces them apart?
questions.explanation: Packages group classes into namespaces, so com.a.Utils and com.b.Utils can coexist.

questions.question: A text editor was creating a Font object per glyph, exhausting memory; the fix caches Font instances and shares one per distinct typeface — which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Sharing immutable intrinsic state across many contexts minimizes memory: the Flyweight pattern.

questions.question: `Animal a = AnimalShelter.adopt("cat")` returns the right subclass while client code never writes `new Cat()` — which pattern hides the concrete class?
questions.explanation: The factory chooses and instantiates the concrete class, so clients depend only on the Animal type.
The private constructor plus one shared static instance make Config a singleton — only one instance can ever exist.

questions.question: One program models entities with classes and inheritance while its data pipeline uses map, filter, and lambdas — how is the language's paradigm best described?
questions.explanation: Supporting both object-oriented and functional styles in a single language makes it multi-paradigm.
Circle inherits the unimplemented abstract method; it must override area() — declaring itself abstract would not help, since new Circle() still could not be instantiated.
make_adder returns the inner function add — a higher-order function; invoking it with 3 closes over n=2, giving 5.
The * operator between V objects dispatches to __mul__, building a new V whose x is 3 * 4 = 12: operator overloading.
Overload selection uses the declared type Object, resolved at compile time via static binding — the runtime String value is irrelevant.
who() is overridden, so the call is resolved by the object's runtime type via dynamic binding, printing C — unlike static binding, which would use the reference type.

questions.question:
What does this Python snippet print?
class Counter:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        Counter.count += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
print(a.count)
questions.explanation: The class variable count is shared by all instances, so two constructions make it 2.

questions.question: In Java, String s1 = new String("hi"); String s2 = new String("hi"); what does s1 == s2 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: == compares references; new String creates two distinct objects, so it is false.

questions.question: What does this Python snippet output? x = [1, 2]; y = x; y.append(3); print(len(x))
questions.explanation: y is an alias of x, so appending through y modifies the same list.

questions.question: In Java, Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; what does System.out.println(a == b) print?
questions.explanation: Integers outside the -128 to 127 cache range are distinct objects, so == is false.

questions.question: What does print(type(type)) output in Python?
questions.explanation: Type is a metaclass and is an instance of itself in Python's object model.

questions.question: `String a = new String("x"); String b = new String("x");` — what does `a.equals(b)` evaluate to in Java?
questions.explanation: equals() compares contents, so it returns true even though a == b on the references would be false.

questions.question: `Point a = new Point(); a.x = 1; Point b = a; b.x = 5;` — what is a.x?
questions.explanation: b aliases the same object; assignment copies the reference, not the object.

questions.question: In Java, `int[] arr;` declared as a field but never assigned — what does `arr.length` do?
questions.explanation: Unassigned object fields default to null; dereferencing null throws NullPointerException.

questions.question: In Java, `int n; if (false) n = 1; System.out.println(n);` inside a method — what happens?
questions.explanation: Local variables have no defaults; the compiler flags n as possibly uninitialized.

questions.question: `void bump(int n){ n++; }` called as `int v = 1; bump(v);` — what is v afterward?
questions.explanation: Java passes primitives by value; the caller's variable is unchanged.
